name: Canton Tower
label: Canton Tower
camera_source: Commons cluster (7 photos), weak. Moved 26 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 170 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/584204634: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Canton Tower' (97 m across).
notes: 600 m TV tower and the city's best-known landmark.

text.description:
Canton Tower is a 600-metre observation tower in Haizhu District, and it looks like nothing else on the skyline. Its lattice of columns, rings and braces twists as it rises and pinches in at about the halfway point, which is why locals nicknamed it "Slim Waist". The tower came into use in September 2010, just before the Asian Games that Guangzhou hosted that year. For a short while it was the tallest tower in the world. It was designed by Dutch architects working with the engineering firm Arup, and the twisting shape comes from rotating two ovals, one at the base and one near the top, against each other.

That shape is what makes it so photogenic. The lines of the lattice curve and cross, and the narrow waist gives your picture a natural focal point. You will probably need to tilt the phone upwards and accept that the sides lean inwards a little, which can look quite dramatic. If you want it to look straighter, step back a few paces and zoom in slightly rather than tilting more. Keep a person or a railing in the lower corner to give a sense of scale. If the tower fills the frame, try a vertical (portrait-orientation) shot.
text.geographic_location: Canton Tower stands in Haizhu District, close to Haixinsha Island.
text.directions_text: Metro and bus stations are located underground at the base of the tower, so head for the tower itself in Haizhu District. Once you are in the area, the tower is very easy to see. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in as much of the tower's height as you can from this close. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter, less stretched view of the waist. Telephoto (2x-5x) suits the detail of the lattice and the top section.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Hold the phone upright and tilt it up gently.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it sits centred, or place it on one third line with space beside it. Include a little foreground, such as paving, trees or a railing, to give it depth. For a different view, try a close crop on the waist at 2x or more, where the twist is easiest to see.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the structure stays detailed. If you shoot after dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a wall to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good time, as the sky colours can contrast well with the tower's shape. The tower is probably lit up in the evening, which gives night shots a different look.

text.access_note: The area around the tower is a public space you can walk to, but access to the tower's decks and attractions may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Shamian Island
label: Shamian Island
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6679655: large area 'Shameen' (1028 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Colonial-era island with European buildings and tree-lined streets.

text.description: Shamian Island is a small sandbank island in Guangzhou's Liwan District, and it feels very different from the busy streets around it. It covers about 0.3 square kilometres, roughly 900 m from east to west and 300 m from north to south. The Pearl River runs along its southern edge and a canal separates it from the mainland. In 1859 the island was split between Britain and France, and the old trading mansions, churches and quiet tree-lined pedestrian avenues are still there. That mix is why it photographs so well: long shaded walks, verandahed buildings in various states of repair, and bronze statues dotted around that show scenes from the island's past. Two buildings are worth looking for. Christ Church Shameen dates from 1865, and Our Lady of Lourdes Chapel was completed in 1892. The chapel stands at the French end of the island. Today the island also has hotels, restaurants and souvenir shops, so there is somewhere to stop between pictures. Look for tree-framed avenues, building facades with their verandahs, and the statues, which make good foreground subjects. Take your time, as the best shots are often found by following the quiet side streets.
text.geographic_location: Shamian Island is in Liwan District, Guangzhou. It is bordered by the Pearl River to the south and separated from the mainland by a narrow canal.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the best route to Shamian Island in Liwan District. Once on the island, walk to the phone icon on the map. From there the marked spot is 292 m to the west, a short walk. The island is a pedestrian-friendly place, so it is easy to explore on foot from there. The phone icon on the map is about 290 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes and building fronts. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long tree-lined avenues, and use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details and the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up an avenue so the trees on each side frame the view and the buildings lead the eye into the picture. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the whole avenue, and keep your phone level so the buildings do not lean. For the bronze statues, get close and use portrait mode to separate them from the background. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out details such as verandahs and church facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the main subject, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright sky is washing out the buildings. In shaded avenues, hold your phone steady, and use night mode if you are shooting in dim light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually pleasant, as the light is softer and the island is often quieter.

text.access_note: The island's avenues are public pedestrian streets, but individual buildings, churches and hotels may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Guangzhou Opera House
label: Guangzhou Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '花城广场' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '花城广场' (way/243319596): edge nearest the subject (1576 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10061850: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Guangzhou Opera House' (235 m across).

text.description:
Guangzhou Opera House was designed by Zaha Hadid and opened on 9 May 2010. It was conceived as two rocks washed away by the Pearl River, and the building does look like a pair of large pebbles, with sloping stone-clad sides and no obvious straight lines. That makes it a good subject for a phone. The shapes are bold and the outline reads clearly even in a small picture. The auditorium is concrete, set inside a granite and glass-clad steel frame, and the building took over five years to build. It is the biggest performing centre in southern China.

The best view for most visitors is from the square, 花城广场, rather than the building's own forecourt. From there the opera house sits in a row with the library and the museum, and the Canton Tower rises behind. The square is spacious, so you can fit in the whole group of buildings and often keep crowds out of the frame. If you want a closer, more abstract picture, walk over to the building itself. The double-curved stone form is reflected in the water pool in front of it, which is worth a few frames of its own.

Take a wide shot first to show the setting, then move in for the curves and the reflection. Keep the phone level so the big curves look natural rather than leaning.
text.geographic_location: In Guangzhou, with the Pearl River to the south, beside the open square of 花城广场 and its neighbouring library and museum.
text.directions_text: Go by taxi or use a map app from central Guangzhou, and search for or ask for 花城广场 or 广州大剧院 (show the Chinese names on your phone). From there the opera house is about 2 minutes on foot to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole row of buildings. Then use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the opera house alone. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Canton Tower behind or for the stone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 花城广场. The opera house as one part of a row with the library and museum, with the Canton Tower in the background. The opera house is to the west of you. From here you see it as one part of a row with the library and the museum, and the Canton Tower in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the buildings up with a horizontal line so the curves look natural. Leave open space in the foreground to show how big the square is. If you want a different view, go to the building's own forecourt and shoot the curved stone form with its reflection in the water pool.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the opera house to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone and sky keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your arms against your body, or rest the phone on a ledge, to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good choice, as the light is softer on the stone. Early morning is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the building are generally open to the public, but check the official site before you go, especially if you want to go inside, as interior access and photography depend on events.

name: Chen Clan Ancestral Hall
label: Chen Clan Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '聚贤堂' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '聚贤中学(康园校区)' (way/520784948): middle (95 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/520935699: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chen Clan Ancestral Hall' (150 m across).
notes: Ornate Lingnan-style academy with carved roofs.

text.description: The Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, also called the Chen Clan Academy, was finished in 1894 with money from Chen families across Guangdong. It was built as a temple for ancestors and a place to prepare young clansmen for the imperial exams. Today it houses the Guangdong Folk Art Museum. The symmetrical complex has 19 buildings, nine halls and six courtyards, linked by corridors and narrow lanes. It photographs well because almost every beam, wall, column and roof ridge is decorated, so there is a good picture in nearly every direction. The ceramic ridge on the Gathering Hall (Juxian Hall) roof is the showpiece. It stretches about 27 metres and carries 224 little figures from traditional dramas, with flying-cod finials at the tips. At the front of the same hall is a stone terrace with carved balustrades. According to several guides, this is a good place for close detail of the stone and iron work, with the roof figures behind. Work through the complex in this order: first the three-arch gate with its plaque, then the courtyards and the terrace, then the lanes. Photography is allowed in most areas, but flash and tripods are restricted. It is still used as an ancestral hall, so keep clear of ceremonies and offerings, and expect some side rooms to be closed.
text.geographic_location: In Guangzhou, on Zhongshan 7th Road, beside the Chen Clan Academy metro station. The complex faces south and sits in a built-up street area.
text.directions_text: Take the metro to Chen Clan Academy station, which is right beside the hall on Zhongshan 7th Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the ridge figures and the carved details, and the default lens (1x) for the terrace and balustrade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyards and lanes when you want the whole roofline or a tall wall in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 聚贤堂 (the platform in front of Juxian Hall, looking at the main hall). Close detail of the stone balustrade capitals and the iron openwork railing panels, with the ceramic ridge figures above in the background. It is not inside the complex. The platform in front of Juxian Hall (聚贤堂) is a separate viewpoint that you walk to once you are inside. From that platform you can see the stone balustrade capitals and the iron openwork railing panels close up, with the ceramic ridge figures above them in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Once on the Juxian Hall platform, put a carved balustrade capital or an iron panel in the lower foreground, then tilt up to include the ridge figures. Turn on gridlines and keep the roof ridge level. For a second view, go back to the three-arch gate and shoot the plaque and roof carvings straight-on, centred. In Qingyun Alley, turn the phone upright and use the high grey walls as a tall frame for a portrait.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the detail you want sharp (a carved capital, say), then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the ceramic roof. Turn the flash off. Use portrait mode for people in the lane, not for the carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the site opens, or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the courtyards are quieter. Check the official site for opening days before you go.

text.access_note: This is a museum site and an active ancestral hall, so entry may be ticketed and some rooms may be closed; check the official site before you go.

name: Yuexiu Park
label: Yuexiu Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '五羊石像' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '五羊石像' (way/146688674): middle (18 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Yuexiu Hill'.
notes: Large hillside park at the city's heart.

text.description:
Yuexiu Park covers the slopes of Yuexiu Hill in the Yuexiu District, and it is one of the best-known green spaces in Guangzhou. The hill once marked the northern end of the old walled city, and the park now spreads over about 860,000 square metres. For a phone photographer, the obvious first stop is the Five Rams Sculpture (五羊石像). It was finished in 1960 from more than 130 pieces of granite and is one of the city's emblems. It stands for the five rams of local legend that gave Guangzhou the nickname "City of Rams". Many locals see them as lucky.

The statue works well as a photo because it is large and pale against dark foliage, and the stone steps beside it let you shoot upwards at it with trees around the edges. Go up the steps a little, turn round, and you can include the steps and greenery in the foreground to give the picture depth. If you have time, the old Zhenhai Tower on the hill is a good second subject. It was first built as a guard tower in 1380 and has housed the Guangzhou Museum since 1928. Walk round the statue once before you start, because the light changes quickly under the trees and a small step left or right can clear a distracting branch or a passer-by. Paths here are busy at weekends, so a little patience helps.
text.geographic_location: Yuexiu Park is in Yuexiu District in central Guangzhou, on the hill that once formed the northern edge of the old walled city. The Five Rams Sculpture stands atop Yuexiu Hill.
text.directions_text: No nearby station is listed for this spot, so start from central Yuexiu District and take a taxi or ride-hail to Yuexiu Park, or check a map app for the best route. Once inside, use a map app to find the Five Rams Sculpture. Paths inside the park can be steep in places, so wear comfortable shoes. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the steps and trees around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole sculpture and the greenery in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the rams against the leaves when crowds are in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (stone steps beside the statue, looking up at it). The Five Rams sculpture framed against trees, with the steps and surrounding greenery in the foreground. From there, walk up to 五羊石像 and shoot from the stone steps beside the statue, looking up at it. Your photo shows the Five Rams Sculpture framed against trees, with the steps and surrounding greenery in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving the steps along the bottom edge to lead the eye up. Let a few branches frame the top corners. If you want a different view, the Zhenhai Tower viewpoint gives a wide panorama of rooftops and trees, and the bridge over the lake is another option for a reflection shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against the shade. Try a Live Photo if people are walking past, because you can pick the clearest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning gives cleaner light and fewer people. Late afternoon is softer and warmer.

text.access_note: Yuexiu Park is a public park, but the Zhenhai Tower and Guangzhou Museum may charge entry and close on certain days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Temple of the Six Banyan Trees
label: Six Banyan Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '六榕花塔' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '六榕花塔' (way/146674383): middle (26 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/146674393: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Temple of the Six Banyan Trees' (188 m across).
notes: Buddhist temple with the 57 m Flowery Pagoda.

text.description:
The Temple of the Six Banyan Trees, also called Liurong Temple, is a working Buddhist temple in the middle of Guangzhou. Its main landmark is the Flower Pagoda, an octagonal tower about 57 metres tall and named for its colourful exterior. Banyan trees and temple roofs frame the pagoda, so you can get a tall, layered photo without leaving the courtyard.

The temple was first built in AD 537. The pagoda dates from 1097, was rebuilt in 1373 after a fire and restored in 1900. Treat the exact ages as approximate. The name comes from a poem called "Six Banyans", written by Su Shi after a visit.

The best photo is of the front of the pagoda, taken from the courtyard while pointing the phone upwards. This keeps the whole silhouette against the sky and trees. For a second picture, try the classical temple gate with its name board in the foreground and the pagoda behind. Another option is the front of the Mahavira Hall, with banyan trees and incense burners for a quieter, more solemn frame. In summer (roughly June to mid-July) the lotus pond can also make a pretty photo, best in the morning.

One guide says the pagoda cannot currently be climbed, so check on the day; either way, shoot it from the courtyard. Inside the halls, guides advise no flash and no photos of the Buddha statues. Please keep your voice low around people who are praying.
text.geographic_location: The temple is at 87 Liurong Road in Yuexiu District, in central Guangzhou. It is close to several foreign consulates.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so get to 87 Liurong Road in Yuexiu District, central Guangzhou, by whatever local transport you prefer, and ask for Liurong Temple (六榕寺). From there the middle of the temple grounds is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard so the whole pagoda and the trees around it fit in the frame. If you can step back, the default lens (1x) gives a more natural shape. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the layered roof edges and the colourful details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front of the pagoda, from the courtyard, shooting upward). The full 57-metre octagonal pagoda framed by the banyan trees, shot from below with sky behind it. From here the full octagonal pagoda is framed by the banyan trees, with sky behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone low and tilt it up so the pagoda rises from the bottom of the frame, with branches at the edges. Turn on the gridlines and line the pagoda up with a vertical line. If you want a different view, take the gate (山门) with its name board in the foreground and the pagoda in the distance, or the front of the Mahavira Hall (大雄宝殿) with the banyan trees and incense burners.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the colours do not wash out. Keep the flash off, especially inside the halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sunlight shows off the pagoda's colours. One guide suggests about 8:00 to 10:00, when the courtyard is quieter.

text.access_note: Guides describe entry as free and this is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet inside the halls; check the official site before you go for opening times and any changes.
claims_not_in_sources: Pointing a phone steeply upwards makes tall buildings look as if they lean inwards, so gridlines help you judge this.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep a bright sky from washing out.
Modest dress and quiet behaviour are expected in a Buddhist temple.

name: Guangdong Museum
label: Guangdong Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '花城广场' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '花城广场' (way/243319596): edge nearest the subject (1576 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Box-shaped museum in Zhujiang New Town.

text.description: The Guangdong Museum is the province's general museum of art, nature, culture and history, and its building is a good subject in its own right. The design was inspired by the traditional Cantonese ivory puzzle ball, with layers nested inside one another, and from outside you see a bold, angular, box-like shape. It opened in May 2010 in Zhujiang New Town, replacing the older museum on Wenming Road, and sits in a large open setting with a grass slope around it. That open space is what makes it easy to photograph: you can step back far enough to fit the whole building in. The best-known view is from 花城广场 (Huacheng Square), on the west side of the museum. Take a few frames at different distances, because the facade changes character as you move. A closer shot lets the angular lines fill the frame, while a wider shot shows the museum in its surroundings. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap rather than cropping people out afterwards. Before planning a visit inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum stands in Zhujiang New Town, Guangzhou's newer cultural and business district, which was planned with the Guangzhou Opera House and Guangdong Library close by. The best photo spot is on 花城广场, the open square to its west.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from Zhujiang New Town and go by taxi or on foot, asking for 花城广场 or the Guangdong Museum (广东省博物馆). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the museum, Canton Tower and the two towers into one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the facade. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for a tighter shot of the museum's angles with the towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 花城广场 (west side of the museum). The museum's treasure-box facade with Canton Tower and the East and West Towers behind it in one frame. The museum is to the east of you, and from here its treasure-box facade lines up with Canton Tower and the East and West Towers behind it. For a wider, panoramic view of the full angular facade, you can also try the museum's own forecourt as a second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the museum on one side, with Canton Tower rising in the gap beside it. Keep the phone level so the building's edges stay straight, and leave a little space above the roofline so the towers aren't cut off. Take a second shot from a few steps closer with the default lens (1x), filling the frame with the facade's angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the museum's facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the sky keeps its colour. If the scene is wide, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is confirmed for this view, so go when the light suits you. Soft light earlier or later in the day is generally kinder to the facade than harsh midday sun. If you stay into the evening, try night mode with your phone braced against something solid.

text.access_note: The square and the open ground around the museum are public outdoor space, but entry to the galleries may need an advance booking, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Zhujiang New Town lies in Tianhe District of Guangzhou.
Photography from the square and the museum's entrance forecourt is generally allowed.
Entry to the free permanent galleries usually requires an advance online time slot, and the museum is typically closed on Mondays (hours vary, so check on the day).

name: Huaisheng Mosque
label: Huaisheng Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '光塔路' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '光塔路' (way/445155457): point nearest the subject (322 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/582730182: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Huaisheng Mosque' (111 m across).
notes: Tang-era mosque with a plain white minaret.

text.description:
Huaisheng Mosque is the main mosque of Guangzhou, and it is also known as the Lighthouse Mosque. Its best-known feature is the plain white minaret, about 36 metres tall and built in two storeys. Until the early 20th century it was the tallest building in the city, and in the Middle Ages it worked as a lighthouse for river traffic as well as a wind vane. The mosque has been rebuilt several times, including in 1350 and again in 1695 after a fire. Its earliest origins are a matter of debate, with some old texts pointing to the 7th century.

It photographs well because the smooth, unadorned minaret stands out against the sky, with the mosque gate at its foot. That gives a clean, simple picture with a clear sense of height. From the street in front of the gate you can fit the gate and the minaret into one upright frame. If you have time, the side of the tower with its wide flying eaves makes a good second picture, and the green courtyard is quieter, with trees and stone paths and the minaret behind.

This is a working mosque, so keep a low profile. Photography is generally fine outside and in the courtyard, but not inside the prayer hall. Switch your flash off and ask before photographing any worshippers.
text.geographic_location: Huaisheng Mosque is in Yuexiu District, in the old part of central Guangzhou, on 光塔路 (Guangta Road).
text.directions_text: The mosque is in Yuexiu District, southeast of Ximenkou Station on the Guangzhou Metro, within walking distance. If you would rather not walk, take a taxi to 光塔路 and ask for the mosque's main gate at No. 56. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and minaret together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are tight against the gate, and use telephoto (2x-5x) for the top of the minaret or the roof eaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 光塔路 (in front of the main gate at No. 56, facing the minaret). The mosque's main gate with the white lighthouse-style minaret rising beside it, the classic full-frame postcard view. From here you see the mosque's main gate with the white minaret rising beside it, the classic full-frame postcard view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and use the gridlines to keep the minaret straight; tilting the phone upwards will make the tower lean. Frame the gate with the minaret rising beside it. For a different view, 望月楼 gives a side profile of the tower's wide flying eaves against the sky, and 怀圣寺 (the green courtyard) gives a quieter frame with the minaret in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white minaret to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale surface keeps its detail against a bright sky. Keep the flash off, and do not use the phone inside the prayer hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the gate is open, and avoid Friday around noon, when access is restricted for congregational prayers. Early morning or late afternoon is often calmer on the street.

text.access_note: This is a working mosque with restricted access at times, especially around Friday noon prayers. Opening times can vary, so check on the day.

name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
label: Sacred Heart Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '一德路' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '一德路' (way/496390317): middle (91 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/542890833: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sacred Heart Cathedral' (83 m across).

text.description: Sacred Heart Cathedral, known locally as the Stone House, is a Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral on Yide Road in Guangzhou's old district. Almost everything is granite: walls, pillars and both towers, which is unusual for a cathedral anywhere. The twin towers rise about 53 metres, and the building was finished in 1888 after 25 years of work, much of it done by hand. The site was once the residence of the Qing viceroy, and the façade was modelled on a church in Paris. That makes it a good subject for a phone. The pale stone, pointed arches and symmetrical towers read clearly even in a small screen photo. The photo here is a street view rather than the usual plaza shot. Stand on Yide Road on the arcade side and look back towards the cathedral. The old arcade buildings in the foreground set everyday Guangzhou against the Gothic stonework, and that contrast is what makes the picture. If you want the classic symmetrical view with both spires, take it from in front of the cathedral. A closer view of the stone walls and side entrance also works for a detail shot or a photo with a person against the granite. Keep the towers upright in the frame and leave a little space around them, so you can crop later without cutting off the tops.
text.geographic_location: In Guangzhou's old district, on the north bank of the Pearl River, at 56 Yide Road (一德路56号). The street view is taken from Yide Road itself.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the old district on the north bank of the Pearl River and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Sacred Heart Cathedral, 56 Yide Road (一德路56号). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the arcade and the cathedral together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer and make them stand out against the street. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of arcade in the frame, as it makes the towers look smaller and can lean the vertical lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 一德路 (the arcade side, looking back toward the cathedral). The cathedral seen from the street, with traditional arcade buildings in the foreground for an old-city versus Gothic contrast. On the arcade side, and look back to the north-east towards the cathedral. From here the photo shows the cathedral seen from the street, with the traditional arcade buildings in the foreground. The old city sits against the Gothic stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the arcade as a frame: let its edge or columns fill one side of the picture and place the towers on the other. Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the arcade and the tower walls so the verticals stay straight. For the classic symmetrical view with both spires, or a closer shot of the stone walls and side entrance, walk to the front of the cathedral instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral on the screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale granite and sky don't turn white. If people walk through the frame, take a Live Photo or a few quick shots and pick the best.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight suits the pale granite. The cathedral is closed on some days, so check the schedule first.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship, reportedly closed on Mondays and the third Sunday of each month, and photos inside are allowed without flash but not during Mass, so check the official site before you go.

name: Guangzhou International Finance Center
label: Guangzhou IFC
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 48 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 90 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/184738716: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Guangzhou International Finance Center' (93 m across).
notes: 440 m skyscraper known as the Little Waist's neighbour.

text.description:
Guangzhou International Finance Center, also called the Guangzhou West Tower, is a 103-storey skyscraper in Tianhe District. It stands 438.6 m tall and was completed in 2010. It is one half of the Guangzhou Twin Towers and was designed by WilkinsonEyre. It won the RIBA Lubetkin Prize in 2012. Inside are offices, a Four Seasons hotel and an observation deck on floors 99 and 100. It also has a rooftop helipad, and as of 2023 it was the world's tallest building with one.

It photographs well because of its clean, tapering shape and the sheer scale of the glass front. That makes it a good subject for a dramatic upward shot. It also works for a calmer picture, with a bit of foreground such as paving, trees or people to give a sense of size.

The tower is too tall to fit in one frame from close by, so aim for a bold, simple composition rather than the whole building. Keep the phone steady and level so the edges do not lean too much. If you want the top, step back as far as the surroundings allow. Check the official site before you go if you plan to visit the observation deck or hotel.
text.geographic_location: The tower is on Zhujiang Avenue West in Tianhe District, Guangzhou. It is one half of the Guangzhou Twin Towers.
text.directions_text: Head for Zhujiang Avenue West in Tianhe District, Guangzhou, and look for the Guangzhou International Finance Center. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are standing close to a very tall building. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter, less stretched view of the lower floors. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the pattern of the glass near the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Huacheng Square (northern end of the square). The IFC West Tower, the CTF East Tower and the Canton Tower framed together in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edge up with a vertical line to keep it straight. Tilting up makes the sides lean in, so either embrace the effect with the ultra-wide, or step back and use the default lens (1x) held more level. Try a low, close-up shot with a person or a tree at the edge of the frame for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brightest part of the glass to focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the details in the glass do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and brace your arms against your body to hold the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or just after sunset, when the sky still has some colour and the building lights are on, usually gives the most atmospheric picture. On clear days a morning visit can give a clean blue sky.

text.access_note: The observation deck and hotel are inside the building, so check the official site before you go for access details.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing close to a very tall building and tilting a phone upwards makes the vertical edges appear to lean inwards.
The building lights come on in the evening, and the sky holds colour for a short time after sunset.
The stand-here point is north-east of the tower.

name: Guangxiao Temple
label: Guangxiao Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '大雄宝殿' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '大雄宝殿' (way/835505846): middle (76 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/361874090: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Guangxiao Temple' (362 m across).
notes: One of the oldest Buddhist temples in the city.

text.description: Guangxiao Temple is one of the oldest Buddhist temples in Guangzhou, and it is a calm place to take photographs: red walls, grey-green tiled roofs, old pagodas and big shady trees. The main subject is the Mahavira Hall (Daxiongbao Hall). It was first built in 401 and last rebuilt in 1654. It is about 35 metres wide and 13.6 metres high, so it fills a phone frame easily from the courtyard. In front of it stands the Great Compassion Column, which dates from 826. Behind the hall are the Hair Burying Pagoda, a seven-storey Tang-dynasty brick tower of about 7.8 metres, and two small iron pagodas from the 960s. These are said to be the oldest iron towers in China. The temple took its present name in 1482. The best frame is the straight-on view of the hall from the courtyard, with the flowering trees framing the red walls and roof. If you come in the flowering season, roughly February to March, the yellow blossom adds colour. Keep the phone steady and look for symmetry. Please respect the rules inside: photographing Buddha statues is not allowed, flash is not permitted in the halls, and some spots have No Photos signs. Shoot the buildings, courtyards and pagodas from outside.
text.geographic_location: Guangxiao Temple is in Guangzhou, within walking distance to the north of Ximenkou Station.
text.directions_text: Take the Guangzhou Metro to Ximenkou Station. The temple is within walking distance, to the north of the station. Once inside the temple, follow the main path through the halls to the courtyard in front of the Mahavira Hall, which is the recommended viewpoint for the photograph. Check the official site for current entry arrangements before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the hall. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the courtyard is too tight to fit the whole roofline. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof tiles, carved windows and the tops of the pagodas.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in the courtyard directly in front of the hall, on the central axis). The Mahavira Hall's red walls and tiled roof framed by the flowering trees in the forecourt, with the hall filling the frame. For the photograph, the recommended viewpoint at the temple is the courtyard directly in front of the Mahavira Hall (大雄宝殿), on its central axis. From there the red walls and tiled roof fill the frame, with the flowering trees of the forecourt around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the hall with the middle of the screen, so the symmetry looks deliberate. Keep the phone level to stop the pillars leaning. For something different, try the small Hair Burying Pagoda among the trees, shot straight on or from a low angle to show its tiers. The West Iron Pagoda also works shot diagonally, framed by banyan trees and bamboo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the roof. Do not use flash, as it is not allowed inside the halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The yellow trumpet trees flower roughly February to March, which adds colour in front of the hall. Outside the flower season, a quieter time of day gives you cleaner frames without people in front of the hall.

text.access_note: This is an active Buddhist temple and may be ticketed, with photography rules inside the halls, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Quieter times of day usually give cleaner photos with fewer people in front of the hall.
Phone gridlines and tapping to set focus and exposure help with symmetrical building shots.
The yellow trumpet trees flower roughly February to March.

name: Museum of the Mausoleum of the Nanyue King
label: Nanyue King Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/298795705: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of the Western Han Dynasty Mausoleum of the Nanyue King' (208 m across).
notes: Tomb museum with jade burial suit.

text.description:
The Museum of the Mausoleum of the Nanyue King protects the tomb of Zhao Mo, who ruled the Nanyue kingdom from 137 BC to 122 BC. It was found in 1983 in the middle of Guangzhou, on a building site on Elephant Hill, and the museum opened around it in 1988. The tomb lies about 20 metres underground and is built from 750 large stones. Its seven chambers held more than 1,000 burial objects, including a jade garment sewn together with silk thread, which is the star of the collection. The whole complex covers about 17,400 square metres, so there is room to step back and take in more than one view.

For a phone photographer this is a spot of two halves: calm, framed views of the museum site outside, and the displays inside, where rules and lighting can change. Outside, look for clean lines, steps and open sky, and keep the building level in the frame. Inside, take your time with single objects rather than whole rooms, and look for the bronzes and jade, which have strong shapes and textures. Be ready for dim lighting and glass cases, so move around until reflections disappear. Whether photography is allowed inside, and where, can differ from room to room, so follow the signs and staff, and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Yuexiu District, in central Guangzhou, on Jiefang Road. The site sits on Elephant Hill (Xianggang Shan).
text.directions_text: The museum is at 867 Jiefang Road in Yuexiu District, in the centre of Guangzhou. A taxi or other local transport to that address is a sensible option. Show the driver the address or the museum's name. Once you are on the museum grounds, the phone icon on the map is at the middle of the site. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most outdoor views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of a building or a forecourt, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved or architectural details and objects in display cases.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Turn slowly on the spot and frame the museum buildings around you, rather than looking for one single view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with them so verticals stay straight. Hold the phone level and, if you can, step back to include some sky and ground. Inside, fill the frame with one object at a time and shoot at a slight angle to avoid glare on glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright sky or lit display cases wash out the picture. In dim galleries, hold the phone steady with both hands and let night mode work if it switches on. Don't use flash against glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outdoors, soft light on a bright but hazy or lightly overcast day tends to flatter the buildings. Visiting early or on a weekday morning usually means fewer people in your frames. Check the official site for opening times before you go.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening times, any ticket requirements and photography rules.

name: Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall
label: Sun Yat-sen Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Octagonal blue-roofed hall in traditional style.

text.description:
The Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall is a large octagonal building with a blue roof, set in lawns and old trees in the middle of Guangzhou. It was designed by Lu Yanzhi and built between 1929 and 1931, paid for by donations from local and overseas Chinese people in memory of Sun Yat-sen. The hall spans 71 metres without any pillars inside and seats 3,240 people. It stands on the site of the old Presidential Palace, and a statue of Sun Yat-sen was put up in front of the main entrance.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear and the grounds give you several different views. From the main square you can fit the whole octagonal facade and the statue in one frame. For something quieter, go to the northeast corner of the grounds. There a large old kapok tree reaches over the roof edges, and the branches and curved eaves overlap to give a classical look. Walking round the lawns also gives angled views of the hall's sides among century-old trees.

On a phone, take one wide shot of the whole building, then step closer for the eaves and branches. Wipe the lens first, because pavilion roofs and sky show up every smudge. The exterior grounds are the easy part; if you want to go inside, check the rules on signs, as photography indoors is limited to certain areas.
text.geographic_location: The hall is in Guangzhou, in its own grounds with a large front square and lawns.
text.directions_text: The hall is reached from Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall Station on the Guangzhou Metro, so follow the signs from the station towards the grounds. Once you are in the grounds, the northeast corner is a separate suggestion for the kapok tree view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to look up at the eaves with the tree branches around them. Use the default lens (1x) for the full facade from the square. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out roof edges and tile detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then, once in the grounds, walk to the northeast corner as a separate suggestion. From there you can look up or close in at the building's eaves, framed by the branches of a large old kapok tree.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone upwards and let the branches make a frame across the top or one side, with the roof edge crossing underneath. Turn on gridlines and keep the roof lines level so the building does not lean. For a more classic view, walk back to the main square and capture the full octagonal facade with the bronze statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the roof or the sky-lit part of the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the blue roof stays rich. Take a few shots at slightly different angles, because branches make the scene busy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring is the best season, because one guide says the kapok trees flower then. Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light than midday.

text.access_note: The grounds can be photographed from outside, but entering the building is ticketed and indoor photography is limited to designated areas, so check the official site and signs before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light than midday.
Wiping the phone lens first helps avoid smudges showing in the photo.

name: Zhenhai Tower
label: Zhenhai Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '镇海楼' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/146688561: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Zhenhai Tower' (36 m across).
notes: Five-storey Ming-dynasty tower on Yuexiu Hill, now a museum.

text.description:
Zhenhai Tower, also called the Five-Story Pagoda, is a red-walled, five-tier building on the grounds of Yuexiu Park, in central Guangzhou. It was first built in 1380, at the start of the Ming dynasty, and is about 28 metres high, 31 metres wide and 16 metres deep. When it went up it was the tallest building in the city, and for a long time it stood as Guangzhou's symbol, before the Five Goats Statue took that role. Today it houses the Guangzhou Museum.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear: stacked tiers, deep red walls and sweeping roofs, all set against green park trees. The easiest postcard angle is from the front steps and the open forecourt facing the main entrance. Looking up from there, the whole tower fills the frame, with the tree canopy around it. The forecourt gives you room to step back, which matters, because standing too close forces you to tilt the phone and the tower will lean. Keep your phone level, use the gridlines to check the walls are straight, and take a few frames at different distances. People often wander through the forecourt, so wait a moment for a gap if you want a clean shot. Around 16:00 is one guide's suggested time to come. Check the official site before you go if you also plan to go inside the museum.
text.geographic_location: Zhenhai Tower stands inside Yuexiu Park in central Guangzhou, with green trees framing it in the view from the front.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Yuexiu Park in central Guangzhou and head for the tower. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, get to Yuexiu Park by whatever local transport suits you. Once inside, follow the park paths to the front of the tower and the open forecourt. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the forecourt so the whole five-tier tower fits with some trees around it. If you are close to the steps, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean inwards. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the roof corners and the red walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back from there until the whole red-walled building fits in the frame, with green trees on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's walls up with the vertical lines. Leave a little space around the top tier and let the tree canopy frame the edges. Take one wide shot to show the whole building, then step back or zoom in to 2x or more for a tighter version without distortion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out. Take a Live Photo if people are crossing the forecourt, so you can pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 16:00 is one guide's tip for this tower.

text.access_note: The tower stands in Yuexiu Park, which is free to enter, but the tower itself is a museum, so check the official site before you go for opening days and entry rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The forecourt may have people passing through, so you may need to wait briefly for a clear view.
The tower is a museum, so entry to the inside may be ticketed or restricted.

name: Temple of the Five Immortals
label: Five Immortals Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '五仙牌坊' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/363576776: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Temple of the Five Immortals (not operational)' (184 m across).
notes: Taoist temple with the Five Rams legend.

text.description: The Temple of the Five Immortals is a Ming-era temple compound in old Guangzhou, tied to the story behind the city's nickname, the City of the Rams. The legend says five immortals rode in on five coloured sheep carrying five grains, and the sheep turned to stone when the immortals left. That is why the archway is carved with five sheep. The best photo is the entrance archway, carved with the five sheep, set against the green-tiled gate and red walls. It is a tidy, colourful frame that works well on a phone. The present temple dates from 1377 or 1378, under the Ming, and a large bell installed soon afterwards, about 3 metres high and 5 tonnes, is known as the Forbidden Bell because it has not been rung since a plague broke out. The compound no longer works as a Taoist temple, so it feels more like a quiet heritage site than a busy shrine. Once you have the archway, go further in for two more pictures. The Ming rear hall has a double-eaved roof with bracket work that makes good silhouettes. Beside the pond is a large foot-shaped hollow in the red sandstone, said to be the mark of one of the immortals. Rainwater and turtles often collect there, which makes a good close-up. The archway and rear hall are reported to be busier around midday, so aim for the morning if you can.
text.geographic_location: In the old part of Guangzhou, beside the junction of West Huifu Road and Liurong Road.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the West Huifu Road and Liurong Road junction in the old city and look for the Temple of the Five Immortals (五仙观). Once there, the archway is at the entrance in front of the main hall. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the archway. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the courtyard is too tight to fit the gate and walls in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rear-hall roof and the footprint.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the archway with its five carved sheep, framed by the green-tiled gate and red walls. This is the classic entrance shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the archway in the middle, keeping the sides level so the walls don't lean. Wait for a gap in the crowd if you can. For a different view, go inside to the Ming rear hall and shoot its roof and brackets against the sky, or crouch over the footprint-shaped hollow for a close-up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the archway to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and pale stonework don't wash out. Use 2x or 3x for the roof brackets rather than pinching in further, to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before about 10:00, is reported to suit the gate facade because the light comes from the east. Midday tends to be busier at the archway and rear hall.

text.access_note: This is a heritage compound that is no longer an operating Taoist temple; check the official site before you go for opening days and entry rules.

name: Five Rams Statue
label: Five Rams Statue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '五羊石像' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N5500130221 (Five-Ram statue): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Symbol of Guangzhou, the City of Rams.

text.description:
The Five Rams Statue is a stone sculpture of five rams standing on a plinth on a hill inside Yuexiu Park. It works well for phone photos because of where you can stand. The stone steps directly below the statue let you shoot upward, which makes the sculpture look large. You get the rams against the sky, with the tree canopy framing them from behind. The trees also throw dappled light and shadow across the scene, which gives the picture some drama.

Begin on the steps, then step back or sideways to try a second angle. Seen from the side, the rams sit with tree shadows and sky in one frame, which a straight-on shot misses. The statue is free to reach inside the park, but it is a popular stop. Expect people in your shot in the morning, at weekends and on public holidays. Arriving early gives you the best chance of a clear view of the steps. Take a few frames at different heights, because crouching slightly lower makes the plinth and rams look taller. Wipe your lens before you start, as park air can leave it a little smeary.
text.geographic_location: The statue is on a hill inside Yuexiu Park in Guangzhou. The park lies along Jiefang North Road.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Yuexiu Park in Guangzhou. Go in through the park and follow the signs and paths uphill to the Five Rams Statue. The phone icon on the map is on the steps right below the sculpture, so use it for the last stretch. Street numbers for the park can vary, so rely on the phone icon on the map rather than an address. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the steps and tilt the phone upward. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more tree canopy and sky around the rams. Keep the phone level to limit stretching at the edges. For the side view, use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the rams without moving closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you shoot upward at the five rams on their plinth, with sky and tree canopy behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the rams on one of the upper crossing points, leaving sky above them. Shoot upward so the plinth leads the eye to the rams. For a second picture, move to the side of the statue and frame the rams with tree shadows and sky together. Keep your phone steady against your body, as people often pass on the steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rams to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If the picture looks flat, take one frame with Live Photos on in case someone walks through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds build up. One guide says the light turns soft after 4 PM, so late afternoon is a second option.

text.access_note: The statue stands in Yuexiu Park and is free to reach, but check the official site before you go for current park opening times and entry rules.

name: Haizhu Bridge
label: Haizhu Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '海珠广场' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '海珠广场' (way/409091121): middle (153 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1193265530: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Haizhu Bridge' (401 m across).
notes: Historic Pearl River bridge near Haizhu Square.

text.description:
Haizhu Bridge is an iron bridge across the Pearl River, and it was the first bridge ever built across the river in Guangzhou. Work began in 1929 and finished in 1933. The American contractor Markton Company completed it. The bridge was damaged in 1938 and again in 1949, and today it still carries a two-lane road between the two banks. That long history shows in the heavy ironwork, which gives you strong lines to photograph.

A recommended frame is from the slope at its northern end, on 海珠广场 (Haizhu Square). A Guangzhou trip guide calls this slope the best photo position in the area. Looking south, the approach ramp leads the eye along the bridge to the Pearl River beyond. Kapok trees run from the Guangzhou Hotel up to the bridge, and when they are in bloom they frame the view and local photographers come for them.

For a phone, this is an easy spot. The road and ironwork make natural leading lines, and the river gives the picture depth. Wait for a gap in the traffic if you want a clean ramp, and keep to the pavement while you shoot. If you have time, the south bank is a good second viewpoint. Along 滨江西路 you can photograph the bridge with the river in the foreground, which suits sunrise and blue hour when the bridge is lit.
text.geographic_location: Haizhu Bridge crosses the Pearl River in central Guangzhou. Its north end is at Haizhu Square in Yuexiu District, and it runs south towards Jiangnan Avenue in Haizhu District. The Guangzhou Hotel stands near the northern approach.
text.directions_text: Head to Haizhu Square in Yuexiu District, at the north end of the bridge. The bridge itself lies a short walk to the south-east of that point. Check the map once you arrive, because the exact spot is easier to find on screen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the ramp, the bridge and the river together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when the kapok branches are in bloom and you want them arching across the top of the frame. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the ironwork and make the far end of the bridge look closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 海珠广场 (north end of the bridge, on the slope leading up to the bridge). A view south along the bridge's northern approach and ramp, with the bridge and the Pearl River beyond it, framed by blooming kapok trees in season. The slope at the north end of the bridge is the recommended frame. From this area you look south along the northern approach and ramp, with the bridge and the Pearl River beyond. The bridge lies to the south-east of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the ramp's edge or the bridge rail along one of the lines, so the road leads the eye into the picture. In kapok season, hold the phone low and let the blossom frame the top or one side. For a different view, the south bank along 滨江西路 shows the bridge with the river in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. For the lit bridge at blue hour, use night mode and keep your elbows tucked in or rest the phone on a wall or railing. A Live Photo can catch passing traffic, and you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the kapok trees are in bloom for the classic frame. Otherwise, sunrise or blue hour suit the bridge best, particularly from the south bank when it is lit.

text.access_note: Haizhu Square and the bridge approach are open public space and no restrictions were found, but the bridge carries road traffic, so keep to the pavement and check locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Traffic on the bridge is usually lighter early in the morning, so the ramp is easier to photograph without vehicles.
Resting the phone on a wall or railing helps keep night-mode shots steady.
Kapok trees flower only for a short season each year, so the blossom frame will not be available all year.

name: Peasant Movement Training Institute
label: Peasant Movement Inst.
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '棂星门' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '番禺学宫旧址' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/288489004: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Peasant Movement Institute' (177 m across).
notes: Historic Confucian temple site turned museum.

text.description:
The Peasant Movement Training Institute is a museum about Guangzhou's revolutionary past, set in a former Confucian temple first built in the 14th century. From 1923 to 1926 it was a school, and it trained young activists to take political ideas out to the countryside. The institute opened on 3 July 1924, and Mao Zedong directed its sixth and largest class. Today the lecture rooms and dormitories have been recreated as a commemorative site.

It photographs well because the old temple layout still gives you strong shapes: a red wall, a stone bridge over a half-moon pond, and halls with sweeping eaves. The best-known picture is taken at the main gate, 棂星门. Stand in front of it and look up. A kapok tree's canopy and the sunlight sit against the red wall, and the shadows make the frame feel layered. Photo guides also suggest this spot for traditional-style or Hanfu portraits. Kapok flowers only for a short time, roughly March to April, so outside those weeks expect a plainer but still pleasant red-wall view.

If you have time, there are two more frames inside. One is the single-arch stone bridge over the pond, with koi and fallen petals on the water. The other is the kapok tree seen between the two sets of eaves at the 明伦堂 hall, which looks a little like an ink painting. Take photos freely outdoors, but obey any signs inside the halls.
text.geographic_location: The institute is in central Guangzhou, on South Yuexiu Road. It occupies the grounds of an old Confucian temple.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the South Yuexiu Road area in central Guangzhou and ask for the Peasant Movement Training Institute by name. Once inside the grounds, the main gate (棂星门) is the first photo spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and the red wall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole canopy and wall in one frame while looking up. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of flowers against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main gate, looking up at the kapok tree against the red wall). Looking up from the entrance, the kapok canopy and sunlight sit against the red wall at the main gate. Tilt the phone upwards and you will see the kapok canopy and sunlight against the red wall at the main gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone up so the branches fill the top of the picture and the red wall runs down one side. Turn on gridlines and keep the wall's vertical edge on a grid line so it does not lean. For a portrait, have your subject stand a little way in front of the wall with the blossom above them. If you have time, an alternative is the stone arch bridge and pond, or the kapok tree between the eaves of the 明伦堂 hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red wall or the flowers to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the colours. Use portrait mode for Hanfu or traditional-style portraits. Take a few shots, because dappled light changes the look from frame to frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Kapok blooming season (March to April) gives the best flowers. Roughly 10:00-12:00 or 15:00-17:00 has the best light, according to photo guides.

text.access_note: This is a museum site in a former temple, so check the official site before you go for opening days and times, and note that signs inside halls may restrict photography.
